blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content: The suggestion that octonions may provide a useful language for describing elementary particles is almost as old as the Standard Model (SM) itself, see [@Gunaydin:1973rs] and references therein.[^1] Thus, it was observed early on that the 8-dimensional space of octonions, after a complex structure is chosen, splits as ${\mathbb O}={\mathbb C}\oplus{\mathbb C}^3$, with the first factor naturally corresponding to leptons and the second one describing quarks. The subgroup of the group of automorphisms of the octonions $G_2$ preserving this split is precisely the strong gauge group ${\rm SU}(3)$.

The left/right symmetric models
blocks.content:
[]{#sec:left-right label="sec:left-right"}

We now interrupt our representation theoretic discussion to review the left/right symmetric extensions of the SM, as these are most closely related to our formalism. We follow [@DiLuzio:2011mda], see in particular Section 1.3.1.

blocks.title: Spinor fields
Bi-doublet Higgs field
Two Higgs in the adjoint
blocks.content:
As we already said, the Higgs field $\Phi$ cannot break the ${\rm U}(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry. One thus needs additional Higgs fields. The option that currently seems preferred in the literature goes under the name of the minimal left/right symmetric model, see e.g. [@Maiezza:2016ybz]. It introduces two more Higgs fields in the adjoint of each ${\rm SU}(2)_{L,R}$. It also requires neutrinos to be Majorana particles, and provides a natural room for the seesaw mechanism. The adjoint Higgs fields are $(B-L)$ charged and transform in the following representations $$\begin{aligned}
\Delta_L = (1,3,1,+2),

blocks.title: Two Higgs fields in the fundamental
A model with only fundamental Higgs fields
blocks.content: There is also a version of the model with Higgs in the fundamental representations that does not introduce the bi-fundamental Higgs $\Phi$, see e.g. [@Hall:2018let]. Indeed, the two VEV's ([\[fund-H-vev\]](#fund-H-vev){reference-type="ref" reference="fund-H-vev"}) are sufficient to break ${\rm SU}(2)_{L}\times{\rm SU}(2)_R\times {\rm U}(1)_{B-L}$ down to the electromagnetic ${\rm U}(1)_{EM}$. The drawback of this model is that it does not allow for Yukawa-type mass terms. However, such terms can be produced using higher dimensional operators with two copies of the Higgs, see [@Hall:2018let].
